newsitem.title: USA: Investment guru Buffett holds investments steady.
newsitem.headline: Investment guru Buffett holds investments steady.

text.p: Billionaire stock picker Warren Buffett, chairman of Berkshire Hathaway Inc., issued his famed annual letter to shareholders over the Internet for the first time on Saturday, saying his stock portfolio was the picture of inactivity.
"We continue to make more money when snoring than when active," Buffett wrote in his familiar folksy manner to Berkshire shareholders.
"Inactivity strikes us as intelligent behavior," he wrote. The Dow Jones industrial average has continued to set records this year, despite volatility.

"I should emphasize that, as citizens, (Berkshire Vice Chairman) Charlie (Munger) and I welcome change: Fresh ideas, new products, innovative processes and the like cause our country's standard of living to rise, and that's clearly good.
"As investors, however, our reaction to a fermenting industry is much like our attitude toward space exploration: We applaud the endeavor but prefer to skip the ride," Buffett wrote.

Buffett, the Omaha investor who is among the world's richest men and a widely followed stock market guru, issued a mild warning to his company's stockholders not to expect him to match past rates of phenomenal earnings growth.

He said Berkshire's larger equity capital after recent sales of stock to expand its shareholder base tended to dampen returns. Also, "fluctuations in securities markets" will affect growth, and wide profit swings in the company's holdings of catastrophe-reinsurance businesses will impact the bottom line.

Without being specific, Buffett told shareholders he would continue to look for acquisitions but with the goal of only buying companies he considered "inevitables" -- firms whose earnings prospects looked to grow in the long term.

"Obviously many companies in high-tech businesses or embryonic industries will grow much faster in percentage terms than will The Inevitables. But I would rather be certain of a good result than hopeful of a great one," Buffett wrote.

Buffett, ever looking for ways to cut costs, urged shareholders to contact him about whether they preferred receiving the company's information over its World Wide Web site. Shareholders were also to receive mailed copies of its annual report.

According to the annual report, at the end of 1996, Berkshire's stock holdings included 49.5 million shares of American Express Co., 200 million shares of Coca-Cola Co., 24.6 million shares of Walt Disney Co., 64.2 million shares of Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., 48 million shares of The Gillette Co., 30.2 million shares of McDonald's Corp., 1.7 million shares of The Washington Post Co., and 7.3 million shares of Wells Fargo and Co.
